clue.text: Such policemen avoid a uniform approach

definitions.text: Such policemen avoid a uniform approach

parts.words: Such policemen avoid a uniform approach
parts.note: surface reading: officers who refuse to follow one standard method
setter's reading: these detectives literally do not wear a uniform

explanation.surface: A police squad that refuses to do things by the book, each officer working in their own way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Uniform' looks like an adjective meaning standard, but it is the police uniform these officers leave off.
explanation.definitionFit: Detectives who work in ordinary dress rather than official kit are said to be in this kind of attire.

clue.text: Level-headed eminence dead in city of old Navarre

indicators.note: something said to be in another lies inside it, so the dead word goes within the city

parts.note: Pau was the capital of the old kingdom of Navarre, in south-west France
the late so-and-so is someone who has died

explanation.surface: A grand figure of some standing has died in a historic French town.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Eminence' suggests a dignitary such as a cardinal, but here it is a raised piece of land; 'level-headed' means it has a flat top.
explanation.definitionFit: An elevated tract of ground whose summit is flat is a tableland, a high rise with a level upper surface.

clue.text: Seaman has no right to arrest

parts.note: AB, able-bodied seaman, is the standard crossword sailor
O is nought, a zero or none
RT is a common abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: A sailor finds he has no legal power to detain anyone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Arrest' in the surface is a police detention; as the definition it means to halt something in progress.
explanation.definitionFit: To arrest a process is to stop or check it, and calling off a mission midway halts it the same way.

clue.text: This kind of compartment may be OK with men on Southern Region

indicators.note: may be suggests the letters could become something else, so they are rearranged into a new word

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written
SR was the abbreviation for the Southern Region of British Rail

explanation.surface: A railway carriage section is acceptable for the gentlemen travelling on Britain's southern lines.
explanation.walkthrough: British trains once had separate compartments where tobacco was banned; the Southern Region was the British Rail division serving south London and the south coast.
explanation.definitionFit: A railway carriage section where tobacco was forbidden carried this label, describing someone who does not light up.

clue.text: Shelters in the grounds

definitions.meaning: first meaning: sheltered sides away from the wind
second meaning: sediment left at the bottom of a cup or cask

explanation.surface: Huts or cover put up in the park or on an estate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Grounds' looks like the land around a house, but it means dregs, as in coffee grounds.
explanation.definitionFit: Protected sides out of the wind are lees, and the dregs settling in wine or coffee are also lees.

clue.text: Disapproving expression on hearing college instruction

parts.note: tut is the clicking noise of disapproval

indicators.note: on hearing means as heard by the ear, so the college's name is taken by its sound not its spelling

parts.note: Oriel is a college of Oxford University

explanation.surface: A don frowns on learning what a college teaches.
explanation.walkthrough: Oriel is an Oxford college; said aloud it matches the last four letters' ending.
explanation.definitionFit: A session of teaching given to a small group or single student is a form of tuition or guidance.

clue.text: 28 has a carrier for the vestment

parts.note: the answer to 28 across is a kind of record abbreviated EP
a hod is a builder's trough for carrying bricks

explanation.surface: A cross-reference that reads like an item on a delivery list: a carrier for a priestly garment.
explanation.walkthrough: An ephod is the sleeveless garment worn by the high priest in the Hebrew Bible.
explanation.definitionFit: This ancient Israelite priestly apron is a ceremonial robe worn in worship, so it is a liturgical garment.

clue.text: Tedious musical, for an intellectual

parts.note: a long, drawn-out speech is a tedious one
Hair is the 1960s rock musical

explanation.surface: A dull stage show that only a highbrow could enjoy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Musical' looks like an adjective but is the noun: the show Hair.
explanation.definitionFit: Highbrows and aesthetes were mocked in slang for unkempt locks, so the term labels a cultured, bookish person.

clue.text: A leech clumsily using pincers

indicators.note: done clumsily means handled awkwardly and jumbled, so the letters are muddled into another order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A bloodsucking worm awkwardly gripping with claws.
explanation.definitionFit: Chelae are the claws of crabs, lobsters and scorpions, which grip like tongs.

clue.text: Decoration for naval personnel in action at last

indicators.note: the naval personnel are placed in the action word, sitting inside it

parts.note: ado is fuss and bustle, busy action
RN is the Royal Navy
personnel are the men of a force

indicators.note: at last read literally points to the final letter of the little word at

parts.note: the final letter of at

explanation.surface: A medal awarded to sailors who finally saw combat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Naval personnel' serves twice: Royal Navy, then men. They sit between the fuss word and the tail of 'at'.
explanation.definitionFit: An ornament or embellishment that adds beauty is a decoration, as with jewels or trimmings.

clue.text: Who said the church makes illicit liquor?

indicators.note: said means spoken, so the word who counts for how it sounds rather than how it is spelt

parts.note: who, spoken, sounds like these letters
CH is the usual abbreviation for church

explanation.surface: Someone asks who claimed the parish was brewing bootleg spirits.
explanation.definitionFit: American slang for cheap, often bootlegged spirits, especially home-distilled whisky made without a licence.

clue.text: Even tomboys avoid this hiding place underground

indicators.note: the opening words are hiding the answer, which sits concealed inside them across the gap

parts.note: the letters run across the join of the two words

explanation.surface: Even daring girls steer clear of a secret burrow beneath the earth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hiding place' reads as one noun phrase, but 'hiding' signals the concealed letters and 'place underground' is a verb phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: To lay a body in a grave or vault is to bury it, putting it below the earth's surface.

clue.text: Buckles, gold pair, for a spendthrift

indicators.note: as a verb buckles means bends or crumples out of shape, so the letters are twisted into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A pair of gold shoe buckles bought by a wastrel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Buckles' looks like the fastenings on shoes, but as a verb it means bends out of shape.
explanation.definitionFit: The parable's wasteful son squandered his inheritance, so the word names someone recklessly extravagant with money.

clue.text: Apprehension is lifting

definitions.meaning: second meaning: the act of taking up or raising

explanation.surface: Anxiety easing off, like a fog clearing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Apprehension' suggests worry, but it means comprehension here.
explanation.definitionFit: Grasping an idea quickly shows comprehension, and drawing something upward, like a pipe absorbing water, is also this.

clue.text: He misrepresents the copper trader's product

indicators.note: a product is something made by working raw materials, so the letters are worked into a new arrangement

parts.note: Cu is the chemical symbol for copper
taken as written

explanation.surface: A dishonest merchant passes off his copper goods as something else.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Copper' could be a policeman, but it is the metal's chemical symbol.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who slanders or defames others by spreading falsehoods about them misrepresents them maliciously.

clue.text: The sort of device Peter needed after misfire?

definitions.text: The sort of device Peter needed after misfire?

parts.words: The sort of device Peter needed after misfire?
parts.note: surface reading: a safety mechanism for a gun that has misfired
setter's reading: a peter is slang for a safe, so a safecracker's failed blast leaves the strongbox intact

explanation.surface: A man called Peter has a gun that misfires and needs a safety catch.
explanation.walkthrough: Peter is old criminal slang for a safe; a misfire on a safe means the safe has survived.
explanation.definitionFit: A mechanism designed to revert to a harmless state if something breaks down protects against disaster.

clue.text: Sent up caricature to the editor

parts.note: a lampoon is a satirical caricature
ED is the usual abbreviation for editor

explanation.surface: A cartoon mocking someone is posted to the newspaper's editor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sent up' reads as posted, but it means mocked.
explanation.definitionFit: To send someone up is to ridicule them through satire, which is exactly what a mocking skit does.

clue.text: Shell acquires a hard top, for example, very quickly

parts.note: a hardtop is a motor car with a rigid roof
apace means at speed

explanation.surface: A tortoise speeds up after getting a tough new covering.
explanation.walkthrough: A hardtop is a style of car with a fixed metal roof.
explanation.definitionFit: The hard protective upper casing of a turtle, crab or tortoise is its carapace, a bony armour.

clue.text: As president, he shouldn't drop a sitter

definitions.text: As president, he shouldn't drop a sitter

parts.note: surface reading: a fielder who must not spill an easy catch
setter's reading: the person presiding is one whose seat must stay in place

explanation.surface: A cricket club president is warned not to fumble an easy catch.
explanation.walkthrough: A sitter is cricket slang for an easy catch; here it also hints at a seat, which the presiding figure is named after.
explanation.definitionFit: The person who presides over a meeting or company board is its president or head.

clue.text: Unmannerly young man is married to a style of painting

parts.note: a cub is a raw, ill-mannered youth
taken as written
M is the abbreviation for married

explanation.surface: A rude youth has wed a particular school of art.
explanation.definitionFit: Picasso and Braque's movement broke subjects into geometric planes, an early twentieth-century art movement.

clue.text: Being unprincipled, left scent around

indicators.note: turned around means facing the other way, so the joined letters are read from the end back

parts.note: L is the abbreviation for left
an aroma is a scent

explanation.surface: A crook leaves a trail of perfume behind him.
explanation.walkthrough: The left letter and the scent word are joined, then the whole turned round.
explanation.definitionFit: Having no moral standards at all, lacking any sense of right and wrong, describes an unscrupulous person.

clue.text: One of the parasitic creatures the king had more than enough of

definitions.text: One of the parasitic creatures the king had more than enough of

parts.note: surface reading: a bloodsucking eel-like fish

parts.words: the king had more than enough of
parts.note: setter's reading: Henry I of England is said to have died of a surfeit of these fish

explanation.surface: A king grows sick of the parasites around him at court.
explanation.walkthrough: English history says Henry I died in 1135 after eating 'a surfeit of' this fish, against his doctor's advice.
explanation.definitionFit: This jawless eel-like fish fastens onto other fish with a sucker mouth and feeds on their blood.

clue.text: Smutty business at school

definitions.note: used attributively: a Bluecoat school is a charity school

parts.note: blue jokes are smutty ones
Co is the abbreviation for company
taken as written

explanation.surface: Something indecent going on at a school.
explanation.walkthrough: Bluecoat schools are old English charity schools, such as Christ's Hospital, whose pupils wore long blue coats.
explanation.definitionFit: English charity schools named for the long blue uniform coats their pupils wore are known by this name.

clue.text: Set of moral commandments — ten — in manuscript volume

parts.note: a moral code is a set of rules of conduct
X is the Roman numeral for ten

explanation.surface: The Ten Commandments are written in an old handwritten book.
explanation.definitionFit: An ancient book written by hand, bound in pages rather than rolled as a scroll, such as a biblical text.

clue.text: Pedestal for emperor in our museum

indicators.note: the emperor is put in the museum's initials, enclosed between them

parts.note: BM is the British Museum, the national museum for a British setter
Otto was the name of several Holy Roman Emperors

explanation.surface: A plinth for an imperial statue displayed in a national gallery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Our museum' is the British Museum, since the setter writes for a British paper.
explanation.definitionFit: A pedestal is the base or foot on which something stands, its lowest supporting part.

clue.text: Sum left a small child upset

indicators.note: upset means knocked over, and in a down entry tipping the letters over reads them bottom to top

parts.note: L is the abbreviation for left
taken as written
a tot is a toddler

explanation.surface: An amount of money was left to a toddler who is now distressed.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down answer, 'upset' turns the joined letters upside down, reading them bottom to top.
explanation.definitionFit: The whole amount obtained by adding figures together is the sum or aggregate.

clue.text: Surrounded by farm hinds, every second counts

indicators.note: only every second letter counts, so the alternate letters are kept and the rest dropped

parts.note: the even-placed letters of farm hinds

explanation.surface: Among the workers on a farm, every moment matters.
explanation.walkthrough: Hinds here are farm labourers, but the word is only fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Being in the middle of things, enclosed on all sides, is the sense of this preposition.

clue.text: Drug for expedition

explanation.surface: Supplies of medicine packed for a journey into the wilds.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Expedition' suggests a trek, but it also means swiftness, as in expeditious.
explanation.definitionFit: Amphetamine is called this in street slang, and quickness of movement or haste is also this.

clue.text: An unknown church in Devon

definitions.note: names a place: a town in Devon

parts.note: taken as the single-letter article
x is the algebraic unknown
a minster is a large church

explanation.surface: A mysterious place of worship somewhere in the West Country.
explanation.walkthrough: Axminster is a market town in Devon, a county of south-west England, famous for its carpets.
explanation.definitionFit: This East Devon market town, known for the carpets woven there since 1755, lies in that county.

clue.text: Put on a performance for the record

parts.note: to put on extra length is to lengthen or prolong
a play is a theatrical performance

explanation.surface: Staging a show so it can be recorded.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put on a performance' reads as staging a show, but splits into two pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: A vinyl disc longer than a single but shorter than an album, abbreviated EP, has this name.
